The terms of the settlement demanded payments that no reasonable estimate of the defeated country’s capacity could support. Its coal fields were reduced, its merchant fleet surrendered, its foreign investments seized, and a debt of enormous proportions placed upon a population already close to exhaustion. It is easy to say that a nation which began a war must pay for it; it is harder to explain how a nation can pay while its industry is crippled and its currency collapses. The negotiators knew this, I think, but domestic politics forbade candor. The consequence will be felt not only by the vanquished: Europe is an economic whole, and the poverty of one part cannot long be separated from the prosperity of the rest.
